blogs.title: Threats, Panic, and the Persecution Line: The Tenth Circuit’s Hard Look at "Threats-Only" Asylum Claims
blogs.description: This post analyzes the court’s reaffirmation that threats and psychological distress, even when serious and repeated, rarely suffice to establish past persecution in the Tenth Circuit. It compares the panel’s approach to other circuits (notably the Ninth) on when death threats can qualify as persecution, unpacks the court’s reliance on precedent like Karki and Brandy, and considers the practical evidentiary takeaways for documenting physical harm, cumulative effects, and corroboration.

blogs.title: When Politics Is Tangential: Mixed-Motive Nexus After Canon Jimenez v. Bondi
blogs.description: Focusing on the nexus analysis, this post explores how the court found the trafficker’s economic/security motives predominated over petitioners’ partisan activism, rendering political opinion merely “tangential.” It situates the ruling within the ‘one central reason’ framework, discusses proof problems in anti-corruption/whistleblowing-as-political-opinion claims, and offers strategies for tying threats to expressly political animus rather than to interference with criminal enterprises.

blogs.title: Unable or Unwilling, or Just Unreported? The Tenth Circuit Tightens the Reporting Expectation
blogs.description: This post examines the court’s government-protection analysis, emphasizing the weight given to the petitioners’ limited reporting and the state’s prior search/seizure efforts at the property. It contrasts the Tenth Circuit’s approach to the futility-and-danger exception with other circuits’ treatments, and provides practitioner guidance on documenting systemic police corruption, safe reporting attempts, or specific reasons why reporting would be perilous.

blogs.title: Internal Relocation as a Decisive Tool: Short-Term Safety, Family Residence, and Regulatory Reasonableness
blogs.description: Here we assess the court’s internal relocation holding—relying on a three-week rural stay, ongoing family safety, and threats keyed to a neighborhood—to conclude relocation is reasonable. The post critiques the opinion’s brief treatment of 8 C.F.R. reasonableness factors, highlights tensions between economic/administrative burdens and doctrinal standards, and suggests how applicants can build a richer relocation record (including feasibility, work prospects, security reach, and child-centered concerns).

blogs.title: The Perils of Under-Developed PSG Claims: What Wasn’t Briefed in Canon Jimenez
blogs.description: This practitioner-focused post underscores the consequences of not fully briefing a particular social group theory. It canvasses plausible PSG formulations in Colombia-related cases (e.g., witnesses/informants, family of those opposing gangs, “social leaders”) and what evidence is needed to establish particularity, social distinction, and nexus, with examples from Crespin-Valladares and related jurisprudence.

blogs.title: Substantial Evidence as the Silent Decider: Deference and Record-Building in Asylum Appeals
blogs.description: Analyzing the opinion’s deference to the BIA/IJ under the substantial-evidence standard, this post explains why most factual challenges falter on petition for review. It discusses the court’s use of Uanreroro to consult the IJ’s reasoning after a single-member affirmance and offers concrete tips for practitioners to develop contemporaneous reporting, motive evidence, and corroboration to survive deferential review.

blogs.title: Private Violence, Public Alignments: Proving State Complicity in Colombia
blogs.description: This post interrogates the court’s rejection of claims that the persecutors were aligned with Colombia’s government, pointing to the record of police enforcement actions against the property. It outlines the types of country-conditions and case-specific proof needed to show state complicity or acquiescence (patterns of non-enforcement, known collusion, targeted impunity), and reflects on how such showings intersect differently with asylum’s ‘unable or unwilling’ test and CAT’s ‘acquiescence’ standard.

blogs.title: From Campaigning to ‘Snitching’: Calibrating Political-Opinion Claims in Narco/Gang Contexts
blogs.description: This post explores the doctrinal boundary between partisan activism and perceived cooperation with law enforcement. It surveys case law on whether anti-corruption or whistleblowing can constitute political opinion, explains why the court deemed the political element subordinate here, and offers litigation strategies to connect threats to political identity or message rather than to purely instrumental retaliation.
